::: {#exr-octopus-beat-plant}
**A foundry for new functions**

In @sec-linear-combinations we presented examples of some functions used in linear combination: flat(), same(), magnitude(), hillside(). The linear combination strategy is like Lego: build a potentially complicated structure by adding blocks to one another. Almost all children are familiar with the basic Lego bricks, such as ![](www/M3004.png){width=8mm}, ![](www/M3003.png){width=8mm}, ![](www/M3009.png){width=17mm}, and ![](www/M3036.png){width=12mm}. These are analogous to our core modeling functions.

Notwithstanding the popularity of the basic Lego bricks, there are some shapes that cannot be constructed by putting the basic ones together. There are many examples, such as ![](www/M3046.png){width=8mm}, ![](www/M30414.png){width=11mm}, and ![](www/M4600.png){width=11mm}. To make such shapes, one needs to visit the Lego *foundry*, where new blocks are cast. There is an analogous foundry for functions, where it's possible to build entirely new shapes not seen in the core modeling functions.

There is an infinite variety of such special-purpose shapes. This makes the task of choosing one daunting, like looking through the entire Lego catalog; so many possibilities, but which ones to choose? Happily, these special-purpose functions usually appear in only a small variety. And instead of having to set up a furnace to melt down and reshape functions, you can accomplish much by applying just two techniques: `r xf_definition("function multiplication")` and `r xf_definition("pipelining functions")`
:::
